Here's a meandering piece on a topic I've been turning over in my piece:

---

**The strange comfort of unfinished things**

I have a half-painted canvas in my closet. Not hidden away in shame, exactly—more like it's been granted honorary furniture status. It leans against the wall at a slight angle, and sometimes when I'm looking for something, I'll catch a glimpse of it: a swirl of deep blue, a suggestion of a horizon, a few confident strokes of white that were clearly painted on a good day.

I started it three years ago. I know exactly which day, in fact. I had bought supplies with the kind of optimism that only arrives when you've decided you're going to become a different person. That person paints. That person has hobbies. That person doesn't just sit and stare at screens.

The first hour was electric. The second hour was difficult. By the third hour I was painting with my jaw clenched, trying to force something that wasn't coming. I told myself I'd come back to it the next day. The next day turned into next week. Next week turned into now.

And yet I can't bring myself to throw it away.

There's something about an unfinished thing that I find almost holy. A finished thing has been judged, declared complete, pinned down. But an unfinished thing is still in conversation with possibility. It could become anything. It holds, in some quiet way, all the people I might still become.

The canvas isn't going to become a masterpiece. I know that. But I don't need it to. It already did something for me. It was a day when I tried. And on the days when I catch sight of it, it reminds me that trying is something I once did, and could do again.

We live in a culture that worships the finished, the published, the optimized, the shipped. But I think there's underrated wisdom in leaving things half-done. In giving yourself permission to set something down not because you've conquered it, but because you've learned what you needed to learn from it. The canvas in my closet taught me that I don't really love painting. What I loved was the idea of loving painting—the version of myself who did. And that's a fine thing to have learned, even if it cost forty dollars in supplies.
